title: Scenario manager — flow inspiration
intro: Product-first flow gallery for the authoring side of the Essentials 2.0 Scenario manager: creating, editing and retiring reusable scenarios; equipment lists with setup notes; per-scenario access; simple checklists and who fills them; QR feedback checklists on the phone without login; simulator and SP scripts; orientation / pre-briefing material; and per-scenario automatic behaviour. Adding scenarios to a course is covered in courses/05-scenarios, general roles and sharing in the user-management research, and equipment stock in 05-inventory. Sources: Mobbin and Refero. Researched 30 September 2026.
baseline: Today's Essentials SCE (Simulated Clinical Experience) editor is a tabbed form: Details, Objectives, Patient, Briefing, and Equipment & Supplies with setup notes for the tech. It exports to PDF or a Maestro file, its state-based builder is a subset of Laerdal Maestro, and the checklist editor is a cut-down Enterprise Case Manager; scheduling templates can auto-send prep emails and auto-start recording and announcements per phase. Customers still author in Word or on paper, and a checklist window that closes loses its data. The direction is a deliberately basic scenario manager (no new Maestro; SimCreate integration instead), linked to inventory, with simpler sharing, a new interactive orientation/pre-briefing maker, and learner or faculty checklists opened from a QR on the room TV, optionally without login.

jobs.title: Add / edit / delete scenarios
jobs.description: Create from blank vs. template vs. duplicate; structured sections (tabs vs. one long page vs. outline); draft/published; versioning; archive vs. delete

jobs.title: Add an equipment list to a scenario
jobs.description: Picking items from a catalog vs. free text; quantities; "setup notes" for the tech; printable prep sheet

jobs.title: Give access to specific scenarios
jobs.description: Share one template with people/groups/roles; view vs. edit; org library vs. private

jobs.title: Add simple checklists to scenarios
jobs.description: Build a checklist/rubric (items, scoring, required); who fills it, when, and why; reusing items across scenarios

jobs.title: Feedback checklist via QR, no login
jobs.description: QR shown on the room TV opens a form on the phone without an account; anonymous vs. identified; submission confirmation

jobs.title: Add scripts (simulator, SP)
jobs.description: Role-specific scripts/cue cards; branching or state-based steps; per-role view

jobs.title: Add orientation material
jobs.description: Attach or build a pre-briefing (video, slides, interactive walkthrough) shown before the session

jobs.title: Decide automatic behaviour per scenario
jobs.description: Per-template defaults that trigger automation: auto-record, auto announcements, learner tagging, reminders; rule builders ("when X, do Y")

products.name: ClickUp
products.why: The only product covering four jobs: Save as Template with a Share-with choice (All members / Only me / Select people / Admins only) in the same modal, checklists with per-item assignees and Use Template, and a When→Then automation with a plain-language summary and an Active toggle.

products.name: Heidi
products.why: Clinical note templates in a healthcare product: three access cards (Team can use but not edit / Community / Only me) and one-click Duplicate from the library row with an automatic '(Copy)' name. The clearest model for simpler per-scenario sharing.

products.name: Cal.com
products.why: A workflow built once and attached to selected event types, with 'Apply to all, including future event types' and an 'Active on N event types' list card. This is exactly a rule set on the template and applied to every run.

products.name: Shopify
products.why: Draft order line items: Search, Browse and Add custom item in one row, a picker with availability per variant, quantities, and a Notes card beside the list. The best model for an inventory-linked equipment list that still allows free text.

products.name: Arcade
products.why: An interactive walkthrough maker for the orientation job: a create-path fork (record / upload / video to demo), Edit | Preview | Insights tabs with a per-step drop-off funnel, and hotspot text that drives the voiceover and can jump to another step.

products.name: Pitch
products.why: Team-library template authoring with a persistent 'You are editing a template' banner, Publish vs Keep draft and Draft badges, plus per-slide speaker notes in a side panel that keep a presence dot when closed.

products.name: Tally
products.why: A doc-style form builder with Draft/Preview/Publish, required asterisks and inline When/Then logic under a field. Its no-account feedback form with a bare thank-you page is the respondent end state a QR checklist needs.

products.name: Typeform
products.why: The author side of QR distribution: one Share hub with Copy link, email and embed, and a Get the QR code modal with Download for printing or showing on a screen.

products.name: Resend
products.why: The only captured versioning: a Draft badge until 'Publish New Version' with a no-warnings check, and a history drawer where Revert creates a new version and stays in Draft.

products.name: Teachable
products.why: Lesson rows show Empty vs content count beside Publish. An Add content drawer puts media blocks next to a Quiz, which is a graded question builder but adds questions one at a time with no reusable bank.

products.name: Google AI Studio
products.why: Per-role dialogue: colour-coded speaker pills on each line, rename the role once in a side rail, global style instructions kept apart from the lines, and a raw text view. A basic SP/operator script without a state machine.

products.name: Instacart
products.why: A named list with a description built from catalog search: popular tiles before typing, multi-select then Done, a 'Buy it again' tab for reuse, and lock/share on the list header.

products.name: Luma
products.why: Counter-example for the QR job: the host's phone scans the guest's ticket QR. That is the opposite of a learner's phone reading a QR on the room TV, though its confirm-then-toast loop suits staff check-in.

patterns.title: Access is chosen when the template is saved, in plain words
patterns.body: ClickUp puts a Share-with choice (All members / Only me / Select people / Admins only) inside the Save as Template modal, with public sharing off by default. Heidi uses three cards and spells out that Team members can use but not edit. Pitch asks Publish vs Keep draft before a template reaches workspace members. For Essentials this suggests a small visibility setting on the scenario itself (private, my team can use, editors) instead of a separate permissions screen; Heidi's moderated public Community is not needed.

patterns.title: Draft is a visible state; publishing is a deliberate step
patterns.body: Pitch shows a persistent 'You are editing a template' banner and Draft badges, Tally keeps Draft/Preview/Publish in the header, and Resend adds 'Publish New Version' with a no-warnings check and a revert that stays in Draft. Scenarios used by running courses need the same separation: faculty can edit freely while the published version keeps running. None of the flows shows what happens to existing copies or courses on republish.

patterns.title: Create from something that already exists
patterns.body: Heidi duplicates from the library row menu without opening the editor, names the copy '(Copy)' and confirms with a toast. Pitch and Tally fork the blank canvas into 'start from scratch' vs 'use a template'. ClickUp's Save as Template turns a working document into a reusable one and offers 'update existing' vs 'save as new'. This is the direct answer to 'customers author in Word': start from a colleague's scenario, not an empty tabbed form.

patterns.title: Rules attach to the template type and say where they are active
patterns.body: Cal.com's workflow asks 'Which event type will this apply to?', offers 'Apply to all, including future event types' and lists 'Active on N event types'. ClickUp writes the When→Then rule back as a sentence, warns inline when an action will be skipped for lack of access, and has a per-rule on/off toggle. For Essentials that means a short When/Do list on the scenario (auto-record at phase start, prep email X days before, announcement), with presets and an 'active on' count, not a general automation product.

patterns.title: Equipment: catalog pick with a free-text escape hatch, notes beside the list
patterns.body: Shopify offers Search, Browse and Add custom item in one row, shows availability per variant in the picker and keeps a Notes card next to the line items. Instacart adds popular tiles before typing, multi-select then Done, and a 'Buy it again' tab to reuse earlier lists. Linking the list to Inventory items while still allowing a custom line covers centers whose inventory is incomplete. The setup notes for the tech belong next to the list, not in another tab.

patterns.title: Scripts sit beside what they cue, labelled by role
patterns.body: Pitch attaches notes to one slide in a side panel and shows a dot when notes exist. Google AI Studio tags each line with a colour-coded speaker, renames a role once for all lines and keeps global style instructions apart from the lines. Arcade's hotspot text drives the narration and has a destination dropdown to jump to another step. Together they give a basic per-phase, per-role script (SP, operator) with simple 'go to' branching, and no Maestro-style state editor.

patterns.title: Orientation is a stack of blocks with authoring, preview and completion in one place
patterns.body: Arcade starts with a choice of source (record, upload, turn a video into a demo), then keeps Edit | Preview | Insights on one project, down to per-step drop-off. Teachable adds blocks from a drawer that groups content blocks and a quiz, and its lesson rows show whether a lesson is empty. For the pre-briefing maker this means an ordered set of blocks (the existing video, text, a click-through of the room or simulator, a short knowledge check) with a learner preview. Completion data per step could show faculty who has done the pre-brief.

patterns.title: Checklists: required items and who fills them are captured; shared item banks are not
patterns.body: Tally marks required items with asterisks and adds When/Then logic inline, ClickUp gives each checklist item an assignee and a Use Template action, and Teachable marks correct answers per question. The products diverge on reuse: ClickUp reuses whole checklists, Teachable adds questions one at a time, and none shows an item bank shared across templates. On the respondent side, Tally's no-account form ends on a bare thank-you page, and Typeform generates a downloadable QR from the same Share hub as the link.

open_questions: Gap: no captured flow shows the whole room-TV loop (QR on a shared screen, then a phone form with no login, then a confirmation). Typeform shows only the author side (link and downloadable QR) and Tally only a no-account form with a thank-you page on desktop. Luma is the reverse case (host scans the guest). A targeted gap fetch found only logged-in in-app surveys. How a no-login submission is tied to the right session and learner (a code in the URL, a name field, a room/session token) is still an Essentials design decision.

Checklist editor: own module or part of the scenario? ClickUp keeps checklists on the item and reuses them via Use Template, Teachable builds a quiz inside a lesson, and Tally builds standalone forms. No product in the report shows one item bank reused across many templates. The evidence leans toward a checklist library that scenarios reference (so one fix updates every scenario), but who owns that library is a product decision.

Versioning vs running courses: Pitch, Tally and Resend make draft vs published explicit, and Resend restores old versions non-destructively. None shows what happens to courses, copies or scheduled sessions that already use a template when a new version is published. This is the same open question courses/05-scenarios raised (pin a version, copy, or live link).

Automation scope: Cal.com and ClickUp only automate emails, assignees and fields. Nothing in the report sets physical-room actions (auto-record, room announcements, learner tagging) per template, and today these live on scheduling templates. Decide whether they move to the scenario, stay on the schedule, or the scenario supplies defaults that the schedule can override.

Equipment and Inventory: Shopify's picker shows availability per variant, which is tempting, but stock and check-out belong to 05-inventory. Decide whether the scenario list shows availability for the scheduled date, or only item identity and quantity plus the tech's setup notes, with printing/prep sheets left to Inventory.
